text: Lesson 29 got order-api and order-worker running inside the cluster, but nothing outside it can reach order-api yet, and anything the worker writes to disk vanishes the moment its pod is rescheduled. This lesson closes both gaps, then collects every object this app needs into one Helm chart.

An Ingress for orders.harrowcreek.dev routes external HTTP traffic to the exact same order-api Service built in Lesson 29. The Ingress doesn't replace that Service -- it sits in front of it, and the Service still does the actual work of selecting which pods receive the traffic.

order-worker writes temporary export files to /data before uploading them, so a PersistentVolumeClaim is mounted into its pod spec. Naming a storage class like standard-rwo triggers dynamic provisioning -- the cluster creates the backing PersistentVolume automatically; nobody pre-creates one by hand, the pattern Chapter 5 already covered.

helm create order-app builds the standard chart skeleton, and all four objects -- both Deployments, the Service, the PVC, and the new Ingress -- move into its templates folder, with hard-coded values like image tags and replica counts replaced by expressions that pull from one values.yaml file instead of being duplicated across every manifest.

helm install order-app deploys the full production-sized release straight from the chart's defaults. A second install, with --set overrides and a values-staging.yaml file, produces a deliberately smaller staging release from the exact same chart source -- the per-environment values pattern Chapter 6 introduced, now applied to a real two-service app.

With order-api, order-worker, routing, and storage all deployed from one versioned chart, Lesson 31 turns to what can still go wrong even on a correctly deployed cluster: a case study in a production outage caused by one pod that was never given a CPU or memory limit.
